title: config/
description: Database, Redis, and Cloudinary setup.
text: database.js connects at import time and exits the process on failure — there is no retry. redis.js creates three lazy clients (presence, publish, subscribe) and stops retrying after five failures, letting the app run without Redis. cloudinary.js configures only when all three keys are present; otherwise uploads fall back to the local folder.

title: controllers/
description: Request handling, one module per area.
text: Controllers own the product rules: no self-connections, no duplicate requests, author-only deletes, poster-only application updates, messaging only between connections or active job pairs. Anything worth telling the user about goes through notifyUser, which stores the notification and emits it into the recipient room.

title: Entry point
description: App setup, route mounting, socket start, listen.
text: The entry requires the database connector (which connects on import), declares permissive CORS with credentials, serves uploads/ statically, answers /health and /api/health without auth or DB waits, mounts the API routers, hands the HTTP server to the socket initializer, and listens on PORT. trust proxy is set for rate limiting behind a proxy.

title: backend/
description: Express API plus the socket server, in one process.
text: One Node process serves HTTP and realtime together: index.js mounts the route modules, starts the socket server on the same HTTP server, and listens. Everything protected goes through the auth guard; uploads branch into Multer before reaching their controllers. Libraries used here: @socket.io/redis-adapter, Socket.io Redis adapter, bcryptjs, better-auth, cloudinary, Cloudinary, cookie-parser, cors, dotenv, express, Express, express-rate-limit, ioredis, jsonwebtoken, mongoose, Mongoose, multer, Multer, multer-storage-cloudinary, nodemailer, Nodemailer, socket.io, Socket.io, validator.

title: middleware/
description: Auth guard, rate limits, and upload handling.
text: The guard reads the jwt cookie first and falls back to the Authorization header — that fallback is what makes hosted frontends work where third-party cookies are blocked. Limits range from 15 auth attempts per 15 minutes to 60 searches per 5 minutes. Uploads pick Cloudinary storage when keys exist and local disk otherwise, cap files at 10MB, and convert Multer errors into 400 responses instead of crashes.

title: models/
description: Six Mongoose schemas, the database shape.
text: Messages, comments, and job applications are embedded subdocuments, not separate collections. Passwords hash on save with cost 12 and never leave the database (the field is excluded from queries by default). The chat model drops near-duplicate messages at save time and keeps the last-message timestamp fresh for conversation ordering.

title: routes/
description: One Express router per area, mounted under /api.
text: All routers except contact apply the auth guard; register, login, logout, and the contact form stay public. Auth, connection, search, post, and job routes carry rate limits. Avatar, cover, post-image, and document uploads attach Multer middleware for their single field before the controller runs.

title: utils/
description: The Socket.io server.
text: One file owns realtime end to end. Sockets register a user id and join that id as a room, so any process can reach a user by id once the Redis adapter is attached. Presence is tracked twice: a local socket map for instant lookups and a Redis hash so other instances agree. Typing and status broadcasts are never stored; messages always are, with sent, delivered, and read states.

title: Environment variables
description: Every variable the code reads, with placeholders only.
text: Placeholder values only — never commit real secrets. The backend .env.example does not list every name the code reads; the tables below merge the example files with the names found in the sources. Backend | Variable | Required | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | PORT | Yes | Port the server listens on. | | MONGO_URI | Yes | MongoDB connection string. | | JWT_SECRET | Yes | Signs and verifies session tokens. | | FRONTEND_URL | For OAuth | Redirect target after GitHub login. | | REDIS_URI / REDIS_URL | No | Redis URL; falls back to localhost, then no Redis. | | CLOUDINARY_CLOUD_NAME | No | Cloudinary account; without all three keys uploads stay local. | | CLOUDINARY_API_KEY | No | Cloudinary key. | | CLOUDINARY_API_SECRET | No | Cloudinary secret. | | GITHUB_CLIENT_ID | For OAuth | GitHub OAuth app id. | | GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET | For OAuth | GitHub OAuth secret. | | EMAIL_USER / GMAIL_USER | For contact mail | Gmail sender account. | | EMAIL_PASS / GMAIL_APP_PASSWORD | For contact mail | Gmail app password. | | EMAIL_RECEIVER | No | Contact form recipient; defaults to the sender. | | API_BASE_URL | No | Base for local upload URLs; defaults to localhost plus port. | Frontend | Variable | Required | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | VITE_API_URL | Yes | REST base, e.g. http://localhost:5000/api. | | VITE_SOCKET_URL | No | Socket base; derived from the API URL when missing. | Service modules fall back to /api and the socket service to localhost when the variables are missing, but set both explicitly in any hosted setup. title: Hosting notes
description: What vercel.json configures, and the Socket.io caveat.
headings: Can Socket.io run in that setup?
text: Two config files, two different jobs: The **root vercel.json** uses the legacy builds/routes syntax to run backend/index.js as a Node function and route every path to it. It says nothing about the frontend. **frontend/vercel.json** is a single SPA rewrite: any path without a dot serves /, so React Router owns deep links. Neither file provisions MongoDB, Redis, Cloudinary, or mail — those stay external services with environment variables. Can Socket.io run in that setup? Honestly: only with caveats. Vercel Functions serve WebSocket connections (Public Beta since June 2026, last verified 2026-10-11), and Socket.IO is listed as supported — but connections are pinned to one function instance up to its maximum duration, reconnects may land on a different instance, and clients must handle reconnects. The repo's Redis adapter is exactly the right shock absorber for that world, and the socket client already reconnects with backoff. The code comments also reference Render (uptime-ping health endpoints, proxy trust, cross-site cookie notes), so the author has clearly run the backend on a long-lived host too. This project does not claim where the author hosts DevConnect, and the legacy builds syntax in the root config predates the current functions-based configuration style. Last verified 2026-10-11. Official references: WebSockets on Vercel Functions Do Vercel Serverless Functions support WebSocket connections? Socket.IO troubleshooting on serverless

title: Deployment overview
description: What has to run for DevConnect to work.
text: DevConnect needs four external services, two of them optional with degradation: **MongoDB** (required) — every collection lives here. The backend exits on a failed connection; there is no retry. **Redis** (optional, degrades) — presence hash and the Socket.io adapter. Without it, realtime works on a single instance only. **Cloudinary** (optional, degrades) — image and document storage. Without keys, uploads land in the backend uploads/ folder and are served statically by Express. **Email over Gmail SMTP** (optional, degrades) — the contact form answers 503 without credentials. The backend is one long-lived Node process serving HTTP and sockets from the same port; the frontend is a static Vite build talking to it over REST plus sockets. See Environment variables for the full table and Hosting notes for what the repo's vercel.json files actually configure. Last verified against the documented commit on 2026-10-11. This project makes no claim about where the author hosts it.

title: Authentication
description: Email register and login plus GitHub OAuth, on JWT.
text: Authentication is JWT plus bcrypt — better-auth sits in both manifests but no source file imports it. Email users register and log in through the user controller with 30-day tokens; GitHub users arrive through OAuth and get the same token. The guard reads the cookie first and the Bearer header second, which keeps hosted frontends working. One honest gap: the signup page reads a fulfilled matcher off a plain thunk, so its post-submit redirect is unverified — login and session restore follow the same token path and are straightforward.

title: Connections
description: Requests, accepts, lists, and removal.
text: One row per pair, unique on the ordered pair, with a pending, accepted, or rejected state. Sending notifies the recipient; accepting notifies the requester; rejecting only flips the state. Lists return the *other* user, populated for display. Accepted connections are the main gate for chat.

title: Feed and posts
description: Publishing, feed, likes, and comments.
text: Posts carry text, an optional image URL, a code snippet with language, a type, tags, and a collaboration flag. The recent tab pages by cursor; the top tab aggregates like counts over the last week. Code snippets render with syntax highlighting in the post card. Likes and comments both notify the post author.

title: Features
description: What DevConnect does, one page per feature.
text: Seven features, each with a slice diagram from page to model: Authentication Profiles and uploads Connections Feed and posts Jobs Notifications Real-time chat

title: Jobs
description: Listings, resume applications, and status tracking.
text: List views strip applications down to counts and an applied flag; only the poster sees full applications on the detail view. Applying attaches a resume plus up to five extra documents through the document uploader and notifies the poster. Active job pairs (poster plus pending, reviewed, or accepted applicants) may message each other without a connection.

title: Notifications
description: Stored rows plus live pushes, one helper.
text: Every notification is a stored row first — connection requests and accepts, likes, comments, job applications, and new messages — so nothing is lost when the recipient is offline. The same helper then pushes into the recipient room for instant display. Self-actions never notify. The bell catches up over REST with unread counts; live arrivals land through the socket service into the slice.

title: Profiles and uploads
description: Editable profiles with avatar and cover uploads.
text: Profiles mix hand-written fields with synced GitHub data (stats, top repos, skills derived from repo languages). Avatar and cover uploads ride the same Multer-plus-Cloudinary path as post images, with a local fallback. Discovery has two doors: the paged user feed (excluding the user and their connections) and name-or-skill search.

title: Real-time chat
description: Rooms, messages, receipts, typing, and presence.
text: Chat has two doors that stay in sync: socket events for live exchange and REST for history and sending from cold state. Every message is stored with a delivery state — sent when the peer is offline, delivered when present, read when the thread opens. Typing and presence are ephemeral broadcasts; only chat content is durable. The Redis adapter lets any instance reach any user room, so the design survives more than one server.

title: Folder structure
description: Where everything lives and why.
text: Two apps, each with its own layout. The backend groups by technical role — config/, routes/, controllers/, models/, middleware/, utils/ — with the entry file at the root. The frontend groups by UI role — pages/, components/, services/, store/, hooks/, lib/, utils/ — with App.jsx and main.jsx at the src/ root. Uploads and helper scripts (fix_db.js, test-cloudinary.js, dummy.txt) exist in the backend folder without being part of the architecture — the backend pages name them but do not document their contents.

title: Static assets
description: Favicons and social images served as-is.
text: public/ carries the favicon, the social preview image, and the Vite badge — files the build copies untouched. src/assets/ holds only the default Vite logo; the app has no other bundled artwork. User content (avatars, post images, resumes) never lives here — it goes to Cloudinary or the backend uploads/ folder.

title: src/components
description: Shared UI, layout, and feature widgets.
text: The ui/ subfolder follows the shadcn pattern (configured in components.json, new-york style): Radix primitives styled with the cn helper. Feature widgets stay near their feature — posts, jobs, and the bell each own their modals and cards — while layout and the route guard frame every guarded screen.

title: src/hooks
description: Shared React hooks.
text: One hook, one consumer: the chat page uses swipe gestures for mobile navigation between the conversation list and the active thread.

title: frontend/
description: React single-page app, routed and stored client-side.
text: The app boots the theme and the session, then splits into public routes (landing, login, signup, legal) and guarded routes inside the main layout. Every server call flows through a service module built on the shared axios factory; everything live flows through the socket service into Redux slices. Libraries used here: @radix-ui/react-avatar, Radix Avatar, @radix-ui/react-label, Radix Label, @radix-ui/react-scroll-area, Radix Scroll Area, @radix-ui/react-slot, Radix Slot, @reduxjs/toolkit, Redux Toolkit, @tailwindcss/vite, Tailwind Vite plugin, axios, better-auth, class-variance-authority, clsx, date-fns, lucide-react, Lucide, prism-react-renderer, react, React, react-dom, React DOM, react-icons, React Icons, react-redux, React Redux, react-router-dom, React Router, socket.io-client, Socket.io client, tailwind-merge, tailwindcss, Tailwind CSS, @eslint/js, ESLint JS config, @types/node, @types/react, @types/react-dom, @vitejs/plugin-react, Vite React plugin, eslint, ESLint, eslint-plugin-react-hooks, eslint-plugin-react-refresh, globals, tw-animate-css, vite, Vite.

title: src/lib
description: Shared code helpers.
text: One six-line file: cn merges conditional classes without Tailwind conflicts, and every ui/ primitive builds on it.

title: src/pages
description: One screen per route.
text: Pages are thin screens over services and slices: forms dispatch thunks, lists select slice state, and the chat page wires the socket service for typing, presence, and receipts. Note pages/auth/ holds older Login and Signup screens that nothing imports — the router uses the top-level LoginPage and SignupPage instead.

title: src/services
description: One typed client per API area, plus the socket service.
text: Every REST module builds on createApi, so the Bearer token, the 30-second timeout, and the expired-session event behave the same everywhere. Base URLs come from VITE_API_URL with localhost fallbacks; the socket URL prefers VITE_SOCKET_URL, then derives from the API URL. The socket service maps server events straight into slice actions.

title: src/store
description: Central store, one slice per feature area.
text: Most slices use async thunks; the auth slice uses plain thunks instead. Realtime never calls the API layer — the socket service dispatches slice actions directly for messages, notifications, presence, and typing. The serializable check is off, so non-plain values can pass through actions.

title: src/utils
description: Small app helpers.
text: The route guard stores the attempted URL before bouncing to login; the auth pages read it back after a successful sign-in so the user lands where they meant to go.

title: High-level architecture
description: The system in one diagram.
text: The browser holds four pieces: the React app, the Redux store, one service module per API area, and the socket client. The API is Express routes into controllers into Mongoose models into MongoDB. The socket server stands next to the API on the same process: chat and notifications travel over rooms, presence lives in Redis, and everything durable still lands in MongoDB. Uploads leave the request path sideways into Cloudinary (or the local folder when keys are missing); contact mail leaves toward the email service. Both are external services, shown in the Shared layer color. Solid lines are durable writes; dashed lines are ephemeral realtime traffic (typing, presence broadcasts, live pushes).

title: How it works
description: Follow one action through the whole system, step by step.
text: Pick a tab and press Play. Each step lights up the nodes involved and narrates what moves: signing up and logging in on JWT, sending and accepting a connection request, a chat message travelling the socket channel with receipts and typing, a post going up with its image, and a notification stored then pushed live.

title: Introduction
description: A social platform for developers, documented folder by folder.
text: DevConnect is a social platform for developers: register with email or GitHub, build a profile, find developers, exchange connection requests, publish feed posts, post and apply to jobs, receive notifications, and chat in real time. The frontend is a React 19 single-page app (Vite, Redux Toolkit, React Router, Tailwind with Radix UI). The backend is a Node CommonJS app (Express 5, MongoDB with Mongoose, Socket.io with a Redis adapter). The two apps install and run independently — see Project structure. These notes describe what each folder owns and how the folders talk to each other. They never explain code — for behaviour, read the linked sources in the repo itself. Where the repo was unclear, the page says so. Start with Installation, then Project structure, then High-level architecture. Tech stack at a glance The codebase is JavaScript and JSX throughout: a Node CommonJS backend and a Vite-bundled React frontend. Authentication is JWT plus bcrypt — the manifests also declare better-auth, but no source file imports it. The full list lives on the Tech stack page.

title: Installation
description: How to run DevConnect locally.
text: You need Node.js 18 or newer, a MongoDB instance (local or Atlas), and, for the full realtime behaviour, a Redis instance and Cloudinary keys. Uploads and the socket adapter both degrade gracefully without them. Separate terminals — the two apps install independently: The frontend serves on http://localhost:5173 and talks to the backend URL in its own .env. Backend scripts are plain node index.js for both dev and start — there is no watcher; restart the process to pick up changes. Environment values Backend .env (names from .env.example plus the optional names the code actually reads — see Environment variables for the full table): Frontend .env: Only placeholder values belong in these files. Never commit real secrets — the repo's committed uploads/ folder already shows why stray files matter.

title: Project structure
description: Two independent apps, not a workspace monorepo.
text: Despite what the repo README calls it, this is **not a workspace monorepo**. There is no root manifest, no workspace configuration, and no shared packages: backend/ and frontend/ are two independent apps with separate installs, separate lockfiles (pnpm-lock.yaml in backend, package-lock.json in frontend), and separate run commands. Each side is started and installed on its own, and either side can be deployed without the other. The backend/ overview and frontend/ overview describe what each app owns. The repo root holds only docs, vercel.json (backend targeting — see Hosting notes), and the two .env.example templates.

title: Flush worker
description: BullMQ worker that flushes Redis room state to durable Prisma snapshots.
text: The worker reads each dirty snapshot, inserts a new scene revision only when the database is behind, and retains the latest revisions. It touches nothing live: presence and previews never pass through here, so a room can be busy without ever being flushed mid-thought — the debounce decides when a snapshot is durable. Libraries used here: @types/node, tsx, typescript, TypeScript.

title: HTTP server
description: Authenticated HTTP API for scenes, rooms, invites, files, and private library items.
text: Routes live under /scenes, /library, and /room, all behind authentication, plus health and account endpoints. Rooms also issue the presence tickets the browser uses to open its WebSocket connection. Shared room checks live in the route utils; the write path itself lives in backend-common. Libraries used here: cors, CORS, express, Express, zod, Zod, @types/cors, @types/express, @types/node, tsx.

title: apps/
description: The runnable services.
text: Each service lists its workspace dependencies in its own package.json; the diagram shows the main ones. The web editor imports the engine, the shared models, and auth. The HTTP and WebSocket servers share the backend collaboration helpers, and both reach the database and Redis packages. The flush worker touches only Redis and the database.

title: Web
description: Next.js editor, account dashboard, and room access interface.
text: Guest drawings stay on the device in IndexedDB. Signed-in work goes through the room sync orchestrator, which keeps a shared room connection, an IndexedDB draft, and a persistent outbox of committed edits. Committed edits are durable; cursor positions, previews, selections, and laser trails are ephemeral frames that are never stored. Libraries used here: jotai, Jotai, next, Next.js, react, React, react-dom, React DOM, @tailwindcss/postcss, Tailwind PostCSS plugin, @types/node, @types/react, @types/react-dom, eslint, ESLint, eslint-config-next, Next.js ESLint config, tailwindcss, Tailwind CSS, typescript, TypeScript, vitest, Vitest.

title: WebSocket server
description: Authenticated room WebSocket transport for presence, scene changes, selections, and laser trails.
text: The server speaks two protocols over one socket family: presence frames and collaboration frames, each validated and rate-limited. Commits are applied through the shared collaboration service and acknowledged per mutation; previews and selections are fanned out to the room and never stored. One connection entry represents one tab, never one user. Libraries used here: ws, @types/node, @types/ws, tsx.

title: Backend on Render
description: HTTP service, WebSocket service, and flush worker as Render services.
text: All three backend services build with tsc -b and start with node dist/index.js. Only Web Service, Postgres, Key Value, and static sites support free instances, so on the free tier every service here is a Render web service — the background-worker service type is paid-only. **Deploy the HTTP service.** Build tsc -b, start node dist/index.js, listening port from PORT (default 5000). It exposes /health, which is also the keep-alive target. Give it DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, and the auth, origin, ticket, email, and OAuth variables from the environment page. **Deploy the WebSocket service.** Build tsc -b, start node dist/index.js, listening port from WS_PORT (default 8080, a separate variable from PORT). It answers only WebSocket upgrades and exposes no HTTP route. Give it DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, PRESENCE_TICKET_SECRET (must match the HTTP service), WEB_ORIGIN, and WS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS. **Deploy the flush worker as an always-on service.** Same build and start commands. It runs a continuous BullMQ process against DATABASE_URL and REDIS_URL, so it needs paid uptime — pinging cannot run it (see the keep-alive page). Without it, room state stays in Redis and snapshots never become durable revisions. Last verified: 2026-10-11. Free-tier limits change — check the providers before relying on any number. title: Cloudflare
description: What Cloudflare can and cannot do for this project.
text: | Use | Verdict | Cost | | --- | --- | --- | | Frontend on Workers via the OpenNext adapter | Feasible and free-tier friendly, but untested with this app | Free tier | | Cron Trigger keep-alive Worker | Yes — see the keep-alive page | Free tier | | DNS and CDN with a custom domain in front of Render | Optional; verify WebSocket traffic through the proxy first | Free tier | | Express HTTP server on Workers | Not a drop-in — Workers are not a long-running Node runtime | N/A | | ws WebSocket server on Workers | Not a drop-in, same reason | N/A | | BullMQ flush worker on Workers | Not a drop-in, same reason | N/A | | Backend on Cloudflare Containers | Possible, but not free — Containers need the Workers Paid plan and bill per running time, with no inbound raw TCP | Paid | | WebSocket server rebuilt on Durable Objects | Possible as a redesign (SQLite-backed objects are on the free plan), not as a deployment | Free tier, rewrite required | **For the frontend, read Cloudflare's current Next.js guide first.** It may recommend a different adapter for new apps. title: Cold starts and keep-alive
description: Why free services sleep, the hours math, and how to ping them awake.
headings: Option 1: Cloudflare Worker with a Cron Trigger
text: Render spins a free web service down after 15 minutes without inbound traffic, and waking takes roughly a minute. Each workspace gets 750 free instance hours a month, shared by all free web services; spun-down services use no hours, and exceeding the allowance suspends every free service until next month. Render may also restart a free service at any time. The hours math Hours equal services times hours per day times days: | Services awake | Hours/day | Days | Hours/month | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 2 | 24 | 31 | ~1,488 — over the 750 limit | | 1 | 24 | 31 | ~744 — leaves nothing for others | | 2 | 8 | 30 | ~480 — fits with room to spare | Keeping both services awake around the clock is not possible on free. Ping only inside a daily window instead — 8 hours a day for both services costs about 480 hours a month. Ping every 10 minutes, which sits safely under the 15-minute idle limit. Never ping /robots.txt: while a service is spun down, Render answers that path itself and the service never wakes. Target the HTTP service's /health. For the WS service, ping its public HTTP URL — but know what it does: the WS server answers only WebSocket upgrades, so a plain GET gets no application response (checked against the code with a local bare-server test). The inbound connection still counts as traffic; confirm the service really stays awake in the Render dashboard during your window. Option 1: Cloudflare Worker with a Cron Trigger Free and precise. The Worker fetches both URLs on a schedule; both URLs come from env vars. **Convert the window to UTC.** Cron Triggers run in UTC. Subtract your offset from both ends of your 8-hour window — 08:00–16:00 at UTC+2 becomes 06:00–14:00 UTC, written as */10 6-13 * *. Half-hour zones should round the window out to whole hours, and zones with daylight saving need the cron adjusted twice a year. **Deploy with Wrangler and check the first runs.** Trigger changes can take several minutes to propagate. title: Database and Redis
description: Neon Postgres, Upstash Redis, then run the migrations.
text: Postgres is the durable authority and Redis the live one, so give each a managed home: a Neon Postgres database and an Upstash Redis database, both reachable over their TCP connection strings. Do not use Render's free Key Value for rooms — it keeps state in memory only and loses everything on restart. **Create the Neon database and copy its connection string.** It becomes DATABASE_URL for every backend service. The database client throws without it. **Create the Upstash Redis database and copy its connection string.** It becomes REDIS_URL for every backend service. Use the TCP URL, not an HTTP one. **Run the migrations from packages/db.** Run db:emit, then db:migration-check, then db:migrate for a fresh database. For an existing database, verify migration and schema state first instead of resetting it. Last verified: 2026-10-11. Free-tier limits change — check the providers before relying on any number. title: Environment variables

title: Frontend
description: Vercel first, with a Cloudflare alternative.
text: Deploy the web app on Vercel. Set NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL to the public HTTP service URL and NEXT_PUBLIC_WS_URL to the public WebSocket URL — both are baked in at build time, so changing them needs a redeploy. Keep NEXT_PUBLIC_GOOGLE_AUTH_ENABLED as false unless Google OAuth is configured. The frontend can alternatively run on Cloudflare Workers through the OpenNext adapter. Read Cloudflare's current Next.js guide first — it may recommend a different adapter for new apps — and treat this app as untested there until someone verifies sign-in, rooms, and presence against it. Last verified: 2026-10-11. Free-tier limits change — check the providers before relying on any number. title: Deployment overview
description: What runs where, and what is free versus paid.
text: The system splits across four hosts. The browser loads the web app from Vercel, then talks to an HTTP service and a WebSocket service on Render, which read and write Neon Postgres and Upstash Redis. A Render flush worker moves room snapshots from Redis into Postgres. | Service | Host | Cost | | --- | --- | --- | | Web app | Vercel | Free | | HTTP service | Render web service | Free, sleeps when idle | | WebSocket service | Render web service | Free, sleeps when idle | | Flush worker | Render | Paid (needs to run continuously) | | Postgres | Neon | Free tier | | Redis | Upstash | Free tier | Free means limited: Render sleeps idle web services and rations instance hours, Neon and Upstash cap their free tiers. Nothing here is production-grade, and every limit below can change — re-check the linked docs before you rely on a number. Last verified: 2026-10-11. title: Verify and troubleshoot
description: Deployment checks first, then fixes for what usually breaks.
text: Deployment checks **Migrations applied.** db:migrate ran clean against the Neon database from packages/db. **HTTP service answers.** Its public /health URL returns a response, and the scenes API works behind authentication. **WebSocket service upgrades.** A room page connects, presence appears, and commits reconcile across two tabs. **Flush worker running.** Room edits become durable scene revisions in Postgres — not just Redis state. **Web app wired.** The deployed editor points at the deployed API and WebSocket URLs, and sign-in plus invites work end to end. Troubleshooting | Symptom | Likely cause and fix | | --- | --- | | First request slow | Cold start — the service was spun down and takes about a minute to wake. Narrow it with a keep-alive window. | | WebSocket won't connect | Wrong port (WS_PORT, not PORT), wss:// vs ws:// mismatch, or origin not allowed — check WEB_ORIGIN and WS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS. | | CORS or cookie errors | WEB_ORIGIN does not match the deployed web URL, or BETTER_AUTH_URL points at the wrong origin. | | Changes not persisting | The flush worker is not running — room state is sitting in Redis only. | | NEXT_PUBLIC_* change not applied | Those values bake in at build time — redeploy the web app. | Last verified: 2026-10-11. title: End-to-end flow
description: Follow one action through the whole system, step by step.
text: Pick a tab and press Play. Each step lights up the nodes involved and narrates what moves: a guest drawing that never leaves the device, a signed-in save through the HTTP server into the database, or a room edit travelling from one browser through the socket, Redis, and the flush worker into Postgres while cursors and previews take a separate path that is never stored.

title: Folder structure
description: Where everything lives and why.
text: The repo separates things that run from things that are reused. Everything that runs — the editor, the API, the realtime transport, the background worker — lives in apps/. Everything reused by more than one of those — models, engine, database, auth, Redis, validation, UI, configs — lives in packages/. Each maintained source folder carries its own README listing its files and subfolders; the folder pages in this guide quote those lists. Open the apps/ overview for the services and the packages/ overview for the libraries.

title: High-level architecture
description: The whole system in one diagram.
text: The browser holds the editor, a sync outbox, and IndexedDB. Signed-in saves travel through the HTTP server into Postgres. Room work travels through the WebSocket server into Redis, and the flush worker later writes durable snapshots from Redis back into Postgres. Solid lines are durable data — committed elements and database rows. Dashed lines are ephemeral — presence, previews, and other live state that is never stored.

title: Introduction
description: A collaborative drawing workspace, documented folder by folder.
text: This project is a TypeScript drawing application with guest storage on the device, authenticated scenes, real-time rooms, a hand-drawn renderer, and Redis write-behind persistence. These notes describe what each folder owns and how the folders talk to each other. They never explain code — for behaviour, read the linked sources in the repo itself. Where the repo was unclear, the page says so. Start with Installation, then the Monorepo layout, then the High-level architecture. Tech stack at a glance The codebase is TypeScript throughout, running on Node 24 or newer with pnpm workspaces. The drawing engine is custom code on the canvas API — no drawing library appears in any workspace manifest. The full list lives on the Tech stack page.

title: Installation
description: What you need and which commands start the project.
text: You need Node.js 24+, pnpm 11.25.0, PostgreSQL 15+, and Redis. Email delivery is needed for verification and invites; Google OAuth is optional. Setup follows the root README: install dependencies at the repository root, copy the environment examples into place, prepare the database from packages/db, then run the dev command at the root, which starts the web app, the HTTP server, the WebSocket server, and the snapshot flush worker together. By default the editor runs on port 3000 (with the dashboard on the same port), the HTTP API on port 5000, the WebSocket server on port 8080, and Redis on port 6379.

title: Low-level diagrams
description: One diagram per folder, side by side.
text: Every diagram below is the same diagram its folder page shows — reused by id, never redrawn. Solid lines are durable data; dashed lines are ephemeral. Web Engine Common HTTP server WebSocket server Flush worker Redis Backend-common Database Auth

title: Monorepo
description: Runnable services in apps/, shared libraries in packages/.
text: There are two top-level folders. apps/ holds the runnable services: the web editor, the HTTP server, the WebSocket server, and the flush worker. packages/ holds the shared libraries they all build on: element models and protocols, the drawing engine, server-only collaboration helpers, the database client, authentication, Redis access, validation schemas, UI primitives, and the shared tooling configs. Each service is started and checked with its own workspace filter command, and the root dev command starts everything together with build dependencies. See the apps/ overview and the packages/ overview for who depends on whom. Shared tooling The root manifest holds only development tooling — the orchestrator, the compiler, and the formatter every workspace builds through: Libraries used here: prettier, Prettier, turbo, Turbo, typescript, TypeScript.

title: Auth
description: Better Auth configuration, browser auth client, email delivery, and authentication helpers.
text: Signing in is email-based with verification links; Google OAuth is optional. Rooms never take a password or a session cookie over the socket: the HTTP server issues a short-lived presence ticket, and the WebSocket server verifies it during the upgrade before checking room access. Libraries used here: bcrypt, better-auth, Better Auth, dotenv, jsonwebtoken, @types/bcrypt, @types/jsonwebtoken, @types/node, typescript, TypeScript, vitest, Vitest.

title: Backend common
description: Server-only collaboration and access operations shared by HTTP, WebSocket, and worker apps.
text: There is exactly one write path for room data, and all three backend services use it: the commit is checked against the caller's role, replayed mutations are dropped, the batch is validated and reconciled, and the result lands in the live store, falling back to the database when Redis is unavailable. Libraries used here: dotenv, @types/node, vitest, Vitest.

title: Common
description: Platform-neutral element models, collaboration protocols, validation, and reconciliation.
text: Room commits reconcile deterministically per element: both sides apply the same winner-picking rules, so concurrent edits converge without a central lock. The protocol caps everything it carries — elements per commit, preview sizes, selection ids — and the validators enforce those caps on both ends of the socket. Libraries used here: vitest, Vitest.

title: Database
description: The sole Prisma schema, database client, repositories, migration graph, and schema snapshots.
text: Durable room state is a versioned chain of scene revisions, each stamped with its actor. The flush worker appends new revisions only when the stored head is behind and prunes everything but the latest ones. Servers enforce owner, editor, and viewer permissions on every access. Libraries used here: @prisma/orm-postgres, Prisma ORM, dotenv, pg, node-postgres, @prisma/cli-engine, Prisma CLI engine, @types/node, @types/pg, prisma, Prisma CLI, tsx, typescript, TypeScript.

title: Engine
description: Browser-independent drawing geometry, tools, renderer, scene capture, and history.
text: The engine never touches the network or the DOM data layer: tools produce geometry, the scene keeps state and history, and the renderer turns state into sketch-style paths with a seeded randomizer so strokes look hand-drawn but render identically. Frames stay flat and axis-aligned by construction. Libraries used here: vitest, Vitest.

title: packages/
description: The shared libraries every service builds on.
text: The rule from the contributing guide: cross-platform reuse goes in common, server-only reuse in backend-common, authentication in auth, and durable database operations in db. Only five packages take workspace dependencies; the rest stand alone. The diagram shows the main uses.

title: Redis
description: Redis live room state, pub/sub, rate limiting, and write-behind queue integration.
text: Redis is the live authority and Postgres the durable one. Snapshot writes are atomic with a Lua version check; when a write lands, the room joins the dirty set and a coalesced flush job is scheduled — debounced, with a maximum wait, and forced when the last participant leaves. Rate budgets are per connection for ephemeral frames and stricter for commits. Libraries used here: bullmq, BullMQ, ioredis, @types/node, tsx, typescript, TypeScript.

title: Tooling configs
description: Shared ESLint and TypeScript configurations.
text: These two packages hold no runtime code — only the lint and compiler settings the apps and libraries extend. They take no workspace dependencies.

title: UI
description: Shared UI primitives.
text: Nothing under apps/ imports this package today — the web editor builds its UI from its own components. The primitives are documented here so a future page has a place to point at. Libraries used here: react, React, react-dom, React DOM, @types/node, @types/react, @types/react-dom, eslint, ESLint, typescript, TypeScript.

title: Validations
description: Reusable request validation schemas.
text: This is a small package with a single job: keep request shapes in one place so the HTTP routes validate the same way. The HTTP server is its listed consumer. Libraries used here: zod, Zod, @types/node.
